item.title: The Eclipse Is Coming, and Iceland Is Looking for a Break in the Clouds
item.description:
A total solar eclipse will cast a shadow across several European countries on Wednesday. But in Iceland, where eclipse chasers were hoping for one of the best possible views, the unpredictable weather may prove to be a spoiler.

So many Icelanders — and some intrepid visitors — plan to make a game-day decision about where to go to watch the spectacle.

“It’s the worst country to watch an eclipse,” said Margret Brynjolfsdottir, who lives in Iceland’s remote northwest, part of the narrow band of the globe where the moon will completely block out the sun.

As of Tuesday, forecasters were predicting overcast skies and rain across most of Iceland. Ms. Brynjolfsdottir, a physical therapist, planned to watch the eclipse from home, no matter how the sky looks. But Icelanders are used to fickle weather, and many are likely to check the forecast on Wednesday morning and hit the road to find the clearest skies they can.

In short, no one really knows where anyone is going to go.

“We are as prepared as we can be,” said Birna Mjoll Atladottir, who runs the westernmost hotel in Iceland, Hotel Breidavik. The period when the moon completely eclipses the sun — known as totality — will last an impressive two minutes and 10 seconds at her hotel. (Just up the road, on the cliffs at the edge of the country, it will stretch on for another three seconds.)

Ms. Atladottir has cleared two fields around her hotel, erected 10 new portable toilets and ordered a month’s worth of food.

If the weather cooperates, she could get flooded with campers. But if not, all that expensive preparation could be for naught.

“We don’t know anything,” she said, sighing.

This will be Europe’s first total solar eclipse since 1999. On most of the continent, the moon will obscure only a portion of the sun, but parts of Russia, Greenland, Spain and Portugal as well as Iceland are in the path of the total eclipse. (People in Spain will be trying to stay safe in extreme heat.)

That rare moment of darkness will last longer here in the Westfjords, a remote region of northwestern Iceland, than almost anywhere else, excluding the oceans. The Westfjords, which are not on Iceland’s main tourist route, has been gearing up to host the eclipse enthusiasts (also known as umbraphiles, or people who love the shadows).

Visitors began making reservations years ago. Some Airbnb hosts and hotel owners have jacked up their prices; some rooms that usually cost a few hundred dollars are going for thousands.

“Iceland is pretty much sold out,” said Saevar Helgi Bragason, a science communicator who has become the country’s unofficial eclipse czar.

And in recent months, harried officials in the Westfjords and elsewhere have been scrambling to fix roads, boost mobile coverage and reserve the country’s relatively few portable toilets.

Foreign tourists aren’t the main concern, officials said. That’s because most of the roughly 75,000 foreigners set to be in Iceland that day have probably committed to a fixed plan.

Instead, it’s the Icelanders, who are used to spending their summers chasing the sun. Any number of the island’s 400,000 residents — about a third of whom will not be able to see a total eclipse from their homes — could set out to find the best possible view. That could result in gridlock on unpaved, less-traveled rural roads.

“The Icelandic weather doesn’t really allow you to make plans ahead of time,” said Diego Ragnar Angemi, an amateur astronomer who lives in the northwestern corner of the Westfjords, where totality is set to last for some 90 seconds.

Conditions can differ from fjord to fjord, Mr. Angemi said, so even a short drive can change the view completely. “I am going to stay home only if I see that it’s cloudy from here to Reykjavik,” he said.

If there’s sunshine anywhere nearby, he said, “I will take the chance — of course.”

The Westfjords have mostly been spared Iceland’s crush of tourists in megabuses, who come to gaze at the northern lights, soak in hot tubs and pose with hot dogs.

This is the rare unbeaten path. And it shows.

Green hills, unmarked by houses, slope up from the fjords. Phone calls drop as you drive around bends. Big grocery stores are hours away. The biggest village in the southern Westfjords, Patreksfjordur, has about 700 residents, four restaurants, a gas station and a liquor store.

Driving here can be, at best, bumpy. Many roads that lace across fjords are unpaved, pitted with potholes deep enough to chatter even a clenched jaw.

On a normal day, that wouldn’t be a major problem. These aren’t busy roads — a quarter of an hour can pass without another car being seen. Most people know to take it slow.

“But it’s not a normal day,” said Johann B. Skulason, a national police official who is helping to coordinate the work of different agencies as Iceland prepares for the eclipse. He spoke from a command center in Reykjavik that would normally be used for a crisis like a volcanic eruption.

Road crews in the Westfjords have been leveling gravel roads, like the one that stretches out past Hotel Breidavik — Ms. Atladottir’s hotel — toward the western Latrabjarg cliffs, where puffins roost and thousands of eclipse chasers could soon gather.

The crews were cutting it close. On Saturday evening, hours after the first people arrived to pitch a tent outside Hotel Breidavik, workers were laying new gravel.

A nearby hospital and fire department have been staffing up and preparing to send emergency crews out to the cliffs. Telecom companies have been strengthening networks for months. And there may never be a better day for Iceland’s waste management industry.

Jon Thorir Frantzson, the chief executive of the Icelandic Container Association, a private company, said all of his portable toilets — he has about 250 — have been rented for months. “It’s never been like this,” he said.

“It’s crazy to have them there, in the middle of nowhere,” he added. “Dragging them all to the Westfjords? That has never happened.”

Ms. Atladottir got her first booking for this Wednesday 14 years ago. She first thought it was a joke. Who makes a booking so far in advance?

Now, it’s all too real. Her rooms have long been booked, but there was still plenty of space for campers. On Saturday, her phone kept ringing.

“I would like to know if we can make a reservation for the 12th?” a caller asked, the second inquiry in under an hour.

Ms. Atladottir calmly explained that no, they were not taking bookings for campsites, but yes, they had more than enough space.

The caller thanked her, and hung up.

“How are we going to be prepared?” Ms. Atladottir said, laughing. “Are we going to expect 100 people — or 1,000 people — or what?”

By Monday, more than a dozen people had already set up their tents in the field outside her hotel. Whatever happens, it’ll be magical, there on her remote stretch of beach, looking up as the sky darkens briefly into night.

Egill Bjarnason contributed reporting from Husavik, in northern Iceland.

item.title: Zhu Rongji, Former Premier Who Pushed China to a Market Economy, Dies at 97
item.description:
Zhu Rongji, the former Chinese premier who played a pivotal role in guiding his country toward a market-based economy in the 1990s and subsequently into the World Trade Organization, died on Wednesday in Beijing. He was 97.

His death was announced by Xinhua, China’s official news agency, which did not cite a cause, noting only that he died after medical treatment failed to save him.

Mr. Zhu, who worked under Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader at the time, contributed more to liberalizing the Chinese economy and making it more internationally competitive than any other recent leader except Deng Xiaoping. Mr. Zhu’s initiatives propelled rapid growth in China that lasted, with a little slowing along the way, until the housing market began to crash in 2021.

But his measures also set the stage for China’s recent problems with excessive debt and its huge trade surpluses, which have led to trade wars with the United States during President Trump’s terms in office.

A young Communist star in the 1950s, Mr. Zhu was expelled from the party in one of Mao Zedong’s ideological purification campaigns. He spent 20 years in obscurity, including five years as a farm laborer.

Politically rehabilitated after Mao’s death in 1976, he soared to the top levels of government. It was Mr. Deng, China’s paramount leader from the late 1970s until his death in 1997, who plucked Mr. Zhu in 1991 from his position as mayor of Shanghai and brought him to Beijing to oversee the country’s economic modernization.

China’s economy had grown rapidly through the 1980s as officials greatly reduced central planning and curbed the chaos of Mao’s final years. But market reforms faltered after a deadly military crackdown crushed the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989.

Mr. Zhu reinvigorated his country’s embrace of market forces, starting as a vice premier in 1991. Promoted to premier seven years later, he oversaw the privatization of thousands of state-owned enterprises and then led China into the World Trade Organization in 2001.

Xu Bingjin, a top aide to Mr. Zhu during the negotiations to join the W.T.O., said in an interview in 2018 that the talks had been like haggling in a vegetable market.

“We would bargain about the price and eventually reach a compromise — sometimes we fought intensely and even banged the table,” he said.

The eventual deal crafted by Mr. Zhu and his aides was unpopular with many Chinese people, particularly in inland provinces that weren’t as prepared for international competition. Mr. Zhu was widely criticized for agreeing to reduce import tariffs on cars and many other goods to no more than 25 percent from 100 percent or more.

But entry into the W.T.O. meant that Chinese goods also had guaranteed access to Western markets with significantly lower tariffs. Exports soared, and by 2010 China had passed the United States to become the world’s largest manufacturer, according to the United Nations Industrial Development Organization.

At the same time, imports did not grow as fast as expected. Mr. Zhu retired soon after China joined the trade body, and the country’s embrace of market forces slowed.

China began erecting new obstacles to bringing in foreign goods. These included extensive subsidies for Chinese manufacturers and numerous requirements that government agencies and state-owned enterprises buy Chinese-made goods.

Under Mr. Zhu, China promised when it joined the W.T.O. that it would quickly open up government procurement to international competition. But China still has not done so. Beijing leaders have faced objections from inland provinces that oppose letting Western companies compete for their sprawling public works projects. Central government officials have submitted several proposals that other countries have quickly rejected as insufficient.

Robert E. Lighthizer, a longtime Washington trade lawyer who was the trade representative for the United States during Mr. Trump’s first term, said Mr. Zhu outsmarted Western negotiators in securing China’s place in the W.T.O.

“Zhu and China clearly got the better deal,” he said in a 2022 email.

As the trade representative, Mr. Lighthizer waged a trade war with Beijing. He imposed tariffs on many Chinese goods in an effort to claw back access to the American market that Mr. Zhu had negotiated. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. left those tariffs in place, and Mr. Trump raised them after he returned to office in 2025.

As vice premier and then premier, Mr. Zhu also oversaw many domestic policies aimed at making China more efficient and competitive. The two most important policies involved the privatization of thousands of inefficient state-owned enterprises and a far-reaching tax overhaul.

Tens of millions of workers lost their jobs during the privatization drive, with many forced into retirement in their 40s. Mr. Zhu softened the blow by enacting an overhaul of the housing market. A vast number of state-owned apartments were transferred to current and retired employees at a nominal cost. State-owned banks issued mortgages at low interest rates for new homes.

Apartment prices soared as much as twentyfold in many Chinese cities from the 1990s until around 2021. That gave many older workers a sizable nest egg, as well as protection from homelessness.

Under Mr. Zhu’s tax overhaul in 1994, the central government seized a much larger share of taxes collected by local governments. The money bankrolled costly initiatives like broad industrial subsidies and a considerable military buildup.

“If we don’t suitably centralize revenues and strengthen the central government’s finances, we won’t be able to get by,” Mr. Zhu said during a 1993 visit to Guangzhou. “And in the end, the entire country will suffer and be unable to carry on.”

Beijing let local governments borrow more money from banks and financial markets in exchange for transferring a larger share of their tax revenues to the national government. Beijing also lifted restrictions that previously limited how local governments could spend money. And Beijing granted greater discretion to local governments to sell long-term leases on state-owned land to developers.

Local governments proceeded to borrow heavily and sell land leases to raise money for new roads, rail lines and ports.

Mr. Zhu’s “grand bargain” with local governments cleared the way for towns, cities and provinces to gorge on debt and become highly dependent on ever-rising revenues from selling land leases. When China’s real estate market fell into a deep slump in 2021, many developers defaulted on loans and stopped buying land leases. This left many local governments with little money to cover their debts.

Mr. Zhu was born on Oct. 23, 1928, in Changsha, the capital of Hunan Province in southern China. He was orphaned as a small child and raised by two of his father’s older brothers, Zhu Kuanjun and Zhu Xuefang. He went on to excel in school and, in 1947, passed the rigorous entrance exam to the elite Tsinghua University, where he studied electrical engineering. He joined the Communist Party in 1949, the year it won China’s civil war.

Like many economic reformers of the 1990s, Mr. Zhu made a remarkable political comeback from persecution before climbing to the top of the Chinese government. He was working at the State Planning Commission, tracking machinery production, when Mao began his Anti-Rightist Campaign in June 1957, striking back at what he saw as dangerous opposition. The campaign led to the political persecution of 550,000 officials, teachers and other citizens over the next two years.

Mr. Zhu was among them. In the early days of Mao’s campaign, Mr. Zhu had given a three-minute talk at the planning commission that followed the prevailing line in Beijing at the time. But the talk was deemed politically unacceptable after the campaign intensified in October 1957.

“Before October, everyone thought that my opinion was good — after October, they said that your opinion should be reconsidered,” Mr. Zhu said in a speech in 1988.

According to a biography of Mr. Zhu published in 2008 by a state company, he was also deemed an “opportunist in revolution” because he had an unacceptable class background: His maternal grandfather, Yu Zhaokang, had been an imperial official before the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911, pioneering railroad construction in China.

Mr. Zhu was expelled from the Communist Party in April 1958 and demoted several rungs at the commission. But he was allowed to remain there to teach math, physics and chemistry to his colleagues.

His early difficulties set him up for further trouble a decade later during Mao’s Cultural Revolution, when he was sent to labor on a farm for five years. “I have done everything: planted wheat, rice and cotton; herded cattle and sheep; raised pigs; and worked as a cook,” he recalled in his 1988 speech.

When the revolution wound down with the illness and death of Mao in 1976, Mr. Zhu spent two years training power transmission workers. As China’s politics began to thaw, he regained his government rank as a deputy director general — the same level he had held as a rising star 20 years earlier.

Mr. Zhu’s Communist Party membership was retroactively restored in late 1978, with full seniority dating from when he joined the party in 1949. He was named research director for industrial economics at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. According to the 2008 biography, Mr. Zhu watched as academy officials burned his letter of expulsion from the party and the documents that had been used as evidence to condemn him as a rightist.

Mr. Zhu quickly became one of China’s leading economic thinkers on industrial and rural issues. Within five years, he was vice minister of the State Economic Commission.

As his career soared, he began a project that would have long-lasting influence: He founded the School of Economics and Management at his alma mater, Tsinghua. He began training a large cohort of economists and finance experts who went on to fill many top posts for decades. (Xi Jinping, China’s current top leader, has limited the influence of these technocrats, however, by creating Communist Party commissions that took considerable decision-making authority away from government agencies stocked with Mr. Zhu’s protégés.)

Mr. Zhu was a popular lecturer at the university on trade, inflation, economic output and other issues, recalled one of his students, Li Shan, now a prominent Chinese financier who has been active in Hong Kong politics.

Mr. Zhu persuaded Mr. Li to leave a Wall Street career at Goldman Sachs to work at the state-owned China Development Bank in Beijing.

“He is very easygoing. He’d have a big smile,” Mr. Li said in an interview for this obituary in 2022. “Normally, people think he is very serious, very tough. But at school, he was a completely different person.”

After working his way up the economic policy ranks in Beijing, Mr. Zhu became the mayor of Shanghai in 1988. He came under Mr. Deng’s wing soon after.

Starting in late January 1990, the elderly Mr. Deng began spending the first days of each Chinese New Year not in frozen Beijing but in milder Shanghai. There, Mr. Deng had long discussions about Mr. Zhu’s plans to redevelop the Pudong area across the Huangpu River from downtown Shanghai.

The area was occupied by aging, state-owned warehouses and farms. Mr. Zhu envisioned turning it into the modern financial center with skyscrapers that it is today. Mr. Deng not only supported those plans but, after a second visit to Shanghai in early 1991, brought Mr. Zhu back to Beijing as a vice premier with special responsibility for trade and industrial production.

A year later, Mr. Deng elevated Mr. Zhu onto the Politburo Standing Committee — the innermost circle of power in the Chinese Communist Party. Six years after that, Mr. Zhu was premier, a post he held until 2003.

While Mr. Zhu was premier, his son, Levin Zhu Yunlai, was the most visible investment banker at the China International Capital Corporation. C.I.C.C., as it is known, worked with Wall Street banks to list the shares of big Chinese state-owned enterprises on Western stock exchanges.

In addition to his son, Mr. Zhu’s family included Lao An, his wife of seven decades, as well as a daughter, Zhu Yanlai. Hong Kong news media reported in 2019 that Mr. Zhu also had at least one granddaughter, the daughter of Zhu Yanlai.

Li You contributed research.

item.title: This Year’s El Niño Is Huge and Already Changing the World
item.description:
El Niño is the planet’s naturally recurring chaos agent, scrambling weather patterns, spiking global temperatures and typically reaching full strength by December.

But this year’s El Niño, which is expected to be record-breaking, is already strong and having big effects, nudging up global temperatures and causing dry spells and crop failures on multiple continents.

Parts of Panama, normally one of the wettest countries on Earth, haven’t had a major storm since early May. Ethiopia’s fertile highlands are enduring one of their driest summer stretches in four decades. And India had its fifth-driest June since the country’s modern rain records began in 1901.

“This is a good sign that the El Niño response has really kicked in,” said Chris Funk, director of the Climate Hazards Center at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Dr. Funk termed it an “early onset El Niño.”

These on-the-ground consequences reflect the magnitude of the changes in the Pacific Ocean, where El Niños develop when unusually warm waters build up. These episodes occur every two to seven years and have contributed to planetary swings going back millenniums. But this year’s is on track to be the strongest in nearly 80 years of records.

Scientists are debating whether human-caused climate change is tilting the odds toward stronger and more frequent El Niño events. The El Niños of the past few decades have been comparably strong. But the variables that combine to create an El Niño are complex, and some experts argue the recent trend could just be a random signal.

What’s clear is that El Niño’s gyrations are adding to the stronger storms, drier dry spells and fiercer wildfires that global warming is already bringing about. El Niño will magnify those phenomena in some regions and could lift global temperatures to record levels next year, as the heat from the Pacific spreads around the world.

“What we’ll see in 2027 is a sneak peak of what the new normal will be in 2035,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth, a nonprofit research organization. “We’ll see things that have never happened before in our history in terms of temperature, drought conditions, extreme heat.”

El Niño events are measured by looking at sea surface temperatures in a specific rectangular zone of the Pacific Ocean. Temperatures there have soared over the past three months, and forecasts suggest that, by year’s end, they could exceed normal levels by more than they did during the strongest El Niños in modern history, which occurred in 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16.

Between October and December, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says there’s an 81 percent chance that El Niño conditions will be “very strong,” meaning the three-month average temperature in that zone of the Pacific is 2 degrees Celsius, or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, higher than normal. But forecasts show that daily ocean temperatures during that period could spike to more than 3 degrees Celsius above normal.

“Maybe it doesn’t sound that big: three or even four degrees. We see that temperature variation over the course of a day,” said Samantha Stevenson-Karl, an associate professor and climate modeler at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “But the ocean doesn’t change that much. Like, ever.”

The extra heat in the waters of the Pacific affects air temperatures, too. For the first months of the year, 2026 was clearly cooler than 2024, the planet’s hottest year on record. But Dr. Hausfather still gives 2026 a 40 percent chance of being Earth’s warmest year on the books, a sign of how the pendulum could be swinging. According to NOAA, last month tied July 2024 as the world’s warmest July since global record-keeping began in 1850.

El Niño causes big shifts in the winds that blow moist air across the oceans, and the effects on rain-fed agriculture are already emerging in some regions. By the end of the year, El Niño could cause nearly 50 million more people across the globe to experience acute hunger, an increase of roughly a fifth, according to the United Nations World Food Program.

At the western end of the tropical Pacific, El Niño has led to a dry summer in parts of Southeast Asia, delaying the sowing of rice and other crops in Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and the Philippines. In India, monsoon rains have picked up in some regions in recent weeks, though large areas of the country remain in a rainfall deficit.

At the other end of the Pacific, El Niño has delayed planting and disrupted crop growth in Central America. Rainfall in Guatemala was as much as 85 percent below average in July, and the stress on crops has been compounded by well-above-normal temperatures.

In Panama, the dry stretch has raised concerns about operations in the Panama Canal. During the last El Niño, in 2023-24, a severe rain deficit snarled traffic in the waterway, which raises and lowers ships through the locks using water from a rain-fed lake.

As El Niño has gained strength, the Panama Canal Authority has tightened limits on how heavily loaded ships can be while crossing. Officials haven’t ruled out restricting daily transits, according to a statement last week from a spokesman for the canal authority, Octavio Colindres.

It’s hard to predict just how much below normal Central America’s rainfall will be in the coming months, said Steven Paton, who monitors the oceans and atmosphere at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama.

The reason, he said, is that scientists’ computer models are trained on past events. This year’s El Niño is expected to be so much stronger than any episode on record that we can’t be sure how accurately the models will anticipate its effects.

“At the very least, it’s going to be as bad as the worst we’ve seen before, possibly much worse,” Mr. Paton said.

In East Africa, El Niño usually brings heavy rain, and even floods and landslides, from November through January. But when the phenomenon appears earlier in the year, it can suppress rainfall in parts of the region, including western Kenya and Ethiopia.

That’s been the dire reality in recent months, said Chris Shitote, a field scientist based in Nairobi, Kenya, for the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, an agency under the U.S. State Department.

Mr. Shitote and some colleagues recently traveled through Kenya’s western grain-producing counties. The maize harvest was stunningly bad, he said. “It’s something some of us have not seen for the maybe 10 years we’ve been going out.”

Plants that normally grow to be nine feet tall topped out at just five or six feet, Mr. Shitote said. A typical harvest might yield 20 to 30 bags of corn for each acre of field, growers told him. This year, it looks like it could be just one or two bags per acre.

item.title: As Europe Faces Another Heat Wave, Travelers Are Forced to Adapt
item.description:
Standing on a paddle board in late July, Kryssi Whitehurst saw a plume of smoke slowly engulf the sky over a lake in southern France. Miles away, the Gironde wildfire would soon prompt one of the largest peacetime evacuations in French history.

Mrs. Whitehurst, from Britain, had traveled to stay in a cabin at one of the region’s beloved campgrounds on the Atlantic coast with her husband and two young children. When they rushed back from their outing, she said, a black and red cloud filled the sky as ash rained down.

“Everybody looked really, really scared,” said Mrs. Whitehurst, who went teary eyed to the reception desk, where she was assured the red smoke came from preventive fire retardant. Her family spent the next five days compulsively checking the news before they were told to evacuate halfway through their 10-day vacation.

The first half of summer in Europe has featured a grueling series of heat waves and widespread wildfires, which have burned more than 1.3 million acres across the European Union. The Danube and Rhine rivers hit record lows caused by drought from the prolonged heat waves, upending river cruises and forcing operators to cancel or change itineraries with alternative bus transfers and hotel stays.

After the hottest June-to-July period on record in Western Europe, the continent is now in the midst of its fifth heat wave since May. Temperatures are expected to reach 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) or more, initially across parts of France, Spain and Italy, then in Central Europe, where some of the highest temperatures are expected in the Czech Republic, Germany and Poland.

Dozens of travelers told The Times that the sweltering season in Europe led them to reschedule travel dates, cancel tours of outdoor sites like the Roman Colosseum, leave trips early or plan future summer vacations to more temperate locations like Scandinavia or mountainous regions. Several people said they struggled with the lack of air conditioning and that their children or older travel companions experienced heat-related illnesses.

“The oppressive temperatures completely altered our trip, turning a visit to these beautiful destinations into something that felt more like a survival contest,” said Rebecca Hoyt, a clinical social worker from Colorado who visited southern Spain and France in early July. She’s already decided not to return next summer.

Climate factors are increasingly shaping where and how Europeans travel, according to a July report from the European Travel Commission. Eduardo Santander, the travel commission’s chief executive, said that the tourism sector must prepare for long-term shifts in seasonal travel, while strengthening resilience, crisis preparedness and communication with visitors.

Despite the fact that these patterns of extreme heat in Europe have been building for several years, travelers have largely been reluctant to change their plans entirely. Industry leaders say they have not seen a notable shift away from preferred summer destinations in Southern and Mediterranean Europe.

“For the past few years I’ve tried to swear off summer travel to Europe, and yet I keep going back,” said Sabina Piersol, an English teacher from San Francisco who did the “unthinkable” and ended her June trip to Paris three days early because of the heat.

Instead, travel patterns are gradually evolving, pointing toward a growing seasonal shift in demand, said Mr. Santander. Compared to last year, travel interest this year was slightly higher in June, signaling a small shift toward early-summer travel, according to the commission. Winter and spring arrivals to Southern Europe are growing, and Nordic regions are reporting record arrivals, he said.

Heat alone does not typically change immediate hotel demand for destinations in France, where a series of heat waves have forced popular sites like the Louvre and Eiffel Tower to close early, according to the MKG group, a market research firm based in Paris.

The shift is more subtle: In summer 2025, hotel occupancy rose faster in the French mountains than on the coast, according to the firm. Revenue per available room grew by double digits on the northern coastlines of the English Channel and Brittany.

Óscar Perelli del Amo, the chief executive of Exceltur, Spain’s national tourism industry association, said the tourism sector expects 10 percent revenue growth in Valencia and Murcia this year, despite soaring summer temperatures in both areas. In Madrid, international tourist expenditure reached 10 billion euros, or about $11.5 billion, in the first half of 2026, up 11 percent from the same period in 2025.

“I’m not worried about this season,” said Ana Rios, a retired nurse who rents out three vacation properties in Madrid. But if it continues to get hotter each year, she said, tourists — like the locals — will not want to stay in the city in the summer.

Operators in Greece expressed similar concerns. Vitorakis Michail, who runs a tour company on Crete, said that increasing heat waves and higher summer temperatures have gradually changed the profile of visitors to the island. “Over the past three to four years, we have seen a growing number of tourists choosing to visit in September and October instead of the peak summer months,” he said.

As Europe confronts more unpredictable weather patterns and as tourists are increasingly exposed to extreme weather, local hospitality leaders say the wildfire response in France highlights a necessity for future economic stability: clear and precise crisis communication.

On July 26, Sophie Brocas, the prefect of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, strongly urged tourists not to travel to Gironde — an area about twice the size of Delaware — until the fire had been contained and for tourists already in the area to consider relocating to a different destination, since the situation could deteriorate.

A cascade of cancellations struck businesses across the entire region, according to the Union of Trades and Industries in the Hospitality Sector, France’s main hospitality union. Some hotels over 60 miles from the fire saw occupancy rates fall as low as 25 percent, the union said, down from 80 percent during the same time last year.

“Informing people transparently about a genuine risk is essential,” said Arthur Laborde, president of the union’s Landes chapter. “Extending that warning unnecessarily to an entire department can create a second crisis — an economic one — far beyond the area actually in danger.”

A fire that directly impacted 4 percent of the Gironde region caused hotel losses in the first 10 days of around seven million euros — a number that exceeded what every major French wildfire in the past decade combined cost the country’s hotels, according to the MKG Group. Before the fire, the agency reported hotels in the region were outpacing last summer’s turnout.

The firm has tracked the impact of wildfires for the past decade and never detected an effect beyond three miles from a burn perimeter. This time, bookings were down across an entire department, including areas more than 50 miles away, such as the wine region around Saint-Émilion.

Rail service and a major highway south of Bordeaux closed for several days, disrupting access to some cities miles from the fire, such as the bayside town of Arcachon.

“I hope within a few days, the phone will start ringing again,” Gilles Delepaux, a hotel manager in Arcachon, said in early August. He said he had to tell some workers to take days off as cancellations mounted.

Most of the impacted businesses are independently owned and sustain themselves throughout the year on the money they make in July and August, said Mr. Laborde, the union president. The group recently launched a campaign called “Don’t Abandon Us!” to recoup visitors.

On July 28, following progress in containing the fires, Serge Papin, the country’s tourism minister, encouraged people not to cancel their August holidays in unaffected areas and emphasized that the tourism season was not over.

Wendy Smith, a 71-year-old retiree from Palm Springs, Calif., was planning to travel during the second week of August along the Atlantic coast of France, from Brittany to Biarritz. But after the fires, she canceled her train tickets and apartment rentals in three oceanside towns. She instead flew straight from Paris to the southern tip of the country.

“My thought was that an extra tourist, even just traveling through the area, would not be helpful to anyone,” she said.

item.title: Here’s how a special U.S. Navy squadron photographed Spain’s 1905 eclipse.
item.description:
The last total solar eclipse visible from Spain was nearly 121 years ago, and, just like this year, it drew crowds from around the world. Among the spectators for the event, on Aug. 30, 1905, were the crews of three warships sent by the U.S. military to take high-definition photographs of the sun’s corona.

That “Eclipse Squadron,” as The New York Times called the expedition at the time, set sail on July 1 carrying one of the largest cameras then constructed, with a lens worth about $900 — about $34,000 today. Several naval astronomers were onboard the ships — the U.S.S. Minneapolis, U.S.S. Columbia and U.S.S. Caesar — ready to set up the camera near the Porta Coeli monastery in the mountains north of Valencia.

The trip was “a wonderful scientific adventure that brought America and Spain together,” said Vicente Muñoz Gimeno, a historical researcher and journalist in Valencia who recently compiled a report about the Eclipse Squadron.

Arriving several weeks before the eclipse, the Americans were just in time for the 1905 Great Valencia Fair, which is still a tradition to this day in the city. The sailors won a regatta against local rowers and attended a bullfight during the festivities. Then, leading up to the eclipse, they worked with residents to erect their 65-foot refractory telescope.

According to Mr. Muñoz, “The expedition resulted in a unique cultural crossroads, where American sailors and astronomers set up cutting edge equipment among local farmlands, shared traditional dances with the residents of Bétera and Serra, and ultimately captured flawless photographic plates of the inner corona during 106 seconds of totality.”

item.title: Driver Sets Record for Hydrogen-Powered Vehicle at More Than 406 M.P.H.
item.description:
The fastest driver on Earth has set another record.

Andy Green, 64, the only person to break the sound barrier on land, set a record for the fastest land speed in a hydrogen-fueled internal-combustion vehicle on Tuesday, at 406.320 miles per hour (653.909 kilometers per hour). The record, set at the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, was confirmed by the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile, the governing body for motorsports.

“The ground comes at you very, very quickly,” Mr. Green, a former pilot for the Royal Air Force, said in a phone interview on Wednesday. “You’re driving five or six times as fast as on the interstate. Everything happens very quickly.”

Mr. Green was driving a JCB Hydromax — which looks more like a rocket on wheels than a car — “ the fastest hydrogen-powered vehicle of any kind in history,” according to JCB, the British machinery company that manufactured it. Beyond setting a land speed record, the company is hoping to use hydrogen engines in the products it builds, Mr. Green said.

No plumes of smoke were produced by this speed record: Hydrogen powers the vehicle and water comes out of the exhaust.

“This is as zero carbon as it gets,” Mr. Green said.

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the F.I.A. president, called the record a “historic milestone” in a statement. The previous land-speed record for a hydrogen combustion vehicle was 185.5 m.p.h., and was set in 2004 by the BMW H2R vehicle, according to F.I.A.

Mr. Green set the record on a 12-mile track on the Bonneville Salt Flats, a 30,000-acre expanse of hard, white salt crust on the Great Salt Lake Basin in Utah.

“You can physically see the curvature of the earth,” Mr. Green said. “This smooth surface is so long.”

How does it feel to be in a vehicle going 400 m.p.h.? Loud, and with heavy vibrations, Mr. Green said. As he accelerated, he looked farther in the distance, and the markers along the course came at him faster and faster, he said. Around him, there was nothing but white salt. The track seemed to get narrower. All of this is happening as he was sandwiched between two roaring engines in a cockpit that was built to fit his 6-foot-3 frame.

It takes about 72 seconds to get from 50 miles per hour to 400, Mr. Green said.

The Bonneville Salt Flats have been the site of speed races since 1912. Once part of a large prehistoric lake that covered a third of the state, the flats are composed mostly of table salt, according to the U.S. Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Land Management.

Mr. Green said on Wednesday that he had considered himself to be retired from speed racing — until JCB called. In October 1997, he broke the sound barrier on land in the Black Rock Desert of Nevada, driving a jet-powered car at an average speed of 763.035 m.p.h. over two runs. That vehicle was powered by two Rolls-Royce engines from a Phantom fighter jet.

That run broke the overall land-speed record set in 1983 by Richard Noble, a British entrepreneur, who traveled at 633.4 m.p.h. with a jet-powered car.

The JCB Hydromax was not built to rival the 1997 record, according to F.I.A., but rather to set a new fastest speed for a hydrogen vehicle. But, the organization said in a statement, “it has laid down an important marker in the world of motor sport and beyond.”

item.title: A Bright Spot in Colombia as Rescuers Free Quake Victim
item.description:
Sometimes you get lucky.

This is Diana Marcela Troncoso. For almost 30 hours, she was trapped in earthquake debris. She gripped the arm of a Colombian firefighter like a lifeline.

As rescuers worked to free her, a police doctor, Claudia Milanes, monitored Ms. Troncoso’s vital signs, making sure she was hydrated.

At least 181 people died in Colombia after the quake. But not Ms. Troncoso. “Diana! Diana!” the crowd chanted as she was carried out. Some applauded.

In Cali, mountains of debris like this one are now commonplace. Many people are still missing.

Military forces were deployed to help the civil authorities cordon off the hardest-hit cities and to coordinate the search for survivors.

But ordinary citizens pitched in, too. They mobilized to gather supplies, food and hydration for the rescue teams.

Supported by

By The New York Times

Diana Marcela Troncoso, a biomedical engineer, was just one of more than 200 people feared trapped alive on Tuesday in the rubble of Cali, the city perhaps hardest hit by the earthquake that rocked Colombia a day earlier.

As emergency workers labored to find buried victims elsewhere in the city, firefighters from the capital, Bogotá, were able to extricate Ms. Troncoso, who is 31.

To get to her, firefighters had to make their way through a narrow tunnel under over 20 feet of rubble. On the surface, it was over 94 degrees Fahrenheit. In the tunnel, it was even hotter, and electrolyte drinks were kept close at hand.

A crowd of onlookers cheered on the rescuers. They could hear a newly freed Ms. Troncoso cry in pain when she was strapped to a backboard. Then they watched as firefighters carefully navigated the debris field and delivered her to a waiting ambulance.

But with the first 48 hours after a disaster like the quake considered critical, the rescue workers could not afford to linger.

Genevieve Glatsky contributed reporting from Cali, Colombia.

item.title: Afghanistan’s Unhappy Anniversary
item.description:
Afghanistan has a track record of defeating superpowers. The mujahedeen humbled the Soviet Union in the 1980s, and five years ago the Taliban pushed out the United States.

But can Afghanistan’s rulers overcome the discontent of their own people?

With the country on the verge of another all-out war, this time with Pakistan, that is less than certain. Today, my colleague Elian Peltier explains why all the ingredients for things to spiral out of control are there.

By Elian Peltier

The Taliban took over Afghanistan five years ago this week. They pushed out the world’s most powerful army. Yet the mood among Taliban officials I’ve spoken with and soldiers I’ve bumped into at checkpoints hasn’t exactly been celebratory — more like embattled.

On what could have been a triumphant anniversary for the group, the Taliban find themselves in crisis at home and abroad.

They face a conflict just short of open war with neighboring Pakistan. They’re dealing with fresh waves of attacks from armed groups who want to topple them. Add to that mass unemployment, near-total international isolation and growing domestic discontent, and it all amounts to the most serious threats the Taliban have encountered since their victory in 2021.

It’s too early to tell whether all this will escalate in a way that could threaten the regime’s survival. But it has cracked the thin veneer of security and stability that the Taliban herald as their primary achievement since taking over — and their primary selling point to the world.

A tight grip on power — and yet

The Taliban are holding Afghan society in a chokehold that spares no one. Girls and women face restrictions to a degree unseen anywhere else in the world. Religious minorities are witnessing the forced closure of their places of worship. Anyone who voices criticism is repressed.

That grip on power over a country of nearly 45 million people seems immovable. The Taliban collect taxes and are pretty good at it. They are building roads, dams and canals. European countries are desperate to work with them to deport Afghan migrants and asylum seekers. And when someone shuts the door on them, as Pakistan did when it closed its border last year, they open new ones: Afghanistan has increasingly relied on trade with Iran, India and Central Asian states like Uzbekistan.

And yet the signs of trouble that have appeared in recent months are impossible to ignore.

An underequipped Afghan Army waits nervously at the border with Pakistan. Once a sponsor of the Taliban, Pakistan has launched dozens of airstrikes on Afghanistan in recent months; killed 500 civilians since October, according to the United Nations; and threatened to go all in against the Taliban regime, which it accuses of harboring militants who are staging attacks on Pakistani territory.

The mistrust goes both ways: The Taliban have accused Pakistan of supporting the armed groups that have attacked Taliban outposts in Afghanistan’s northeastern province of Badakhshan and are gearing up for a sustained offensive.

Whether, or to what extent, Pakistan is actively supporting anti-Taliban groups is not clear, but suspicions are high enough that a senior Western diplomat with decades of experience working on Afghanistan told me this summer, “This region doesn’t need another proxy war.”

The picture on the domestic front is also grim. The Taliban are struggling to deal with a cascade of humanitarian and economic crises. Nearly four million Afghans have been forcibly returned from Iran and Pakistan since January 2025 — one of the world’s largest episodes of reverse migration in decades. Aid cuts have plunged millions into deeper food insecurity. And UNESCO says the Taliban have deprived 2.4 million Afghan girls of a secondary education — the equivalent of all school-age girls in New York, Mexico City and Moscow combined, forced to stay home indefinitely.

A society can withstand only so much, even under the tightest of grips. At a rare protest in June, demonstrators chanted “Work, education, freedom,” similar to what their Iranian neighbors chanted in 2022. And the leader of a large religious minority warned the Taliban in May: Don’t squeeze Afghan society too much, or it will explode.

The potential to spiral?

The Taliban know the world wants a stable Afghanistan — one that isn’t a source of refugees, opium or terrorism.

The Taliban claim the country no longer poses a security threat to the region or the West. They say that they have cracked down on the Islamic State, and that they want peaceful relations based on trade and diplomacy, including with the U.S.

All of this may have some truth to it. The Taliban don’t want their various crises to spiral. But it also might not be entirely up to them.

All the ingredients for things to get out of control in Afghanistan again are here, analysts say: Growing animosity toward Pakistan and a vast population of unemployed young Afghans are fertile ground for radicalization, especially as economic opportunities are nearly nonexistent. Under the Taliban, Afghanistan is, once again, a pariah state, with barely any allies.

As a foreign military official in Afghanistan put it, the country is no longer the hub for jihadism that it used to be — but it has everything it needs to become one again.

The past five years have brought some predictability and an end to almost two decades of fighting, which many Afghans have welcomed, despite the immense hardship and repression. But Afghanistan remains shattered, and what always looked like a fragile peace is already at risk.

item.title: For Trump, Secret Flight Was a Stunning Ruse. For Putin, ‘a Regular Tuesday.’
item.description:
President Trump’s Air Force One subterfuge was a stunning episode of official deception.

But it pales in comparison to the secrecy surrounding President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, whose activity is shrouded in so much mystery that journalists have tried to track it by assessing the wilting of his office plants.

That is the method some reporters resorted to this year as they worked to ascertain whether the Russian leader’s televised meetings took place when the Kremlin said they did. The apparent reversal of the leaf decay seen in Mr. Putin’s plants suggested that the meetings actually took place in a different order and on different days.

For Mr. Putin, such deceit is par for the course. The White House, by contrast, has been criticized for not revealing Mr. Trump’s secret plane switch on a Turkish tarmac last month until The Washington Post broke the story this week.

“Compared to Russia,” said Mikhail Rubin, a Russian investigative reporter, “this is child’s play.”

Mr. Rubin and other reporters have found that Mr. Putin has outfitted his residences with nearly identical offices so that video footage of meetings does not reveal his location. His security apparatus has developed a presidential train, along with special railroad spurs and secret stations near at least three of his country residences, according to news reports and satellite images.

Government officials are forced to play along, keeping their meetings with Mr. Putin a secret until they are televised — sometimes weeks later — and then pretending they happened on that day.

In Russia, official falsehoods about the president’s whereabouts “are just a regular Tuesday,” said Farida Rustamova, a Russian journalist who covers the Kremlin from exile. She has reported that Mr. Putin’s interlocutors in his televised meetings sometimes speak of outdated events, in at least one case in clothes and a haircut incongruous with other public appearances.

There is even a term of art for those delayed-release Putin meetings among Russian journalists: konservy, or canned goods.

The Kremlin has previously denied deceiving the public about Mr. Putin’s location and did not respond to a request for comment.

Covering Mr. Putin as a New York Times correspondent based in Moscow, I got a sense of the lengths the Russian president goes to in order to hide his movements when I visited Lake Valdai, where he has a country residence, in 2021. Residents told me about a mysterious new railroad line that had been built toward his compound. Satellite imagery showed a new station, with a helipad, that did not appear on timetables or railway maps.

In 2023, a defector from the Russian version of the Secret Service, the F.S.O., asserted that Mr. Putin was using train travel to avoid being tracked. Leaked documents indicated that a secret armored train outfitted for the office of the president, painted like a regular passenger train but complete with a gym, spa and special communications equipment, was used by Mr. Putin himself.

Mr. Putin’s preoccupation with secrecy and security appeared to increase during the pandemic, when he forced officials to quarantine for two weeks to see him and when his isolation made it easier to hide his whereabouts. And it has reached new heights since his invasion of Ukraine in 2022, especially as that country’s drones flew deeper into Russia, helping precipitate mobile internet shutdowns and reportedly curtailing his travel.

In Moscow, there is now speculation that the enormous motorcades racing down city streets that are presumed to be carrying Mr. Putin are actually sometimes decoys, according to Ms. Rustamova. One of my Kremlin-connected contacts in Moscow told me the same.

Mr. Rubin, the investigative journalist, first reported in 2020 that Mr. Putin worked from identical-looking offices in his residences in the Moscow suburbs and in the Black Sea resort of Sochi, allowing the Kremlin to lie about his location. A report last year by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty uncovered more details about that deception effort, highlighting tiny differences between those otherwise identical offices — like the placement of door handles and wall seams — that indicated they were in different places.

Mr. Rubin, who is now based in North Carolina and is deputy editor of the news outlet Proekt, first got a sense of Mr. Putin’s secrecy when he covered the Kremlin for a Russian business newspaper a decade ago. Mr. Rubin once happened to see members of Mr. Putin’s Security Council arriving for a meeting, but his office only announced the gathering days later, as though it was a new occurrence. He came to realize, he said, “that Putin’s public image is made up, it’s an absolute lie from beginning to end.”

For Mr. Putin, the deception is not only about security, but about projecting an air of constant activity and control. The intensity of U.S. press coverage of the president, on the other hand, would have been unimaginable in Russia even before the Ukraine war and the pandemic.

But the Trump administration’s restrictions on the news media and its misdirection surrounding the president’s flight last month still look familiar in some Russian eyes.

“Putin in this sense is a caricature of a figure who has taken everything happening around him to the point of absurdity,” Mr. Rubin said. “Trump, it seems to me, is only starting to move in this direction.”

item.title: Settler Siege of Palestinian Homes Highlights Growing West Bank Chaos
item.description:
Two Palestinian families have been trapped since Sunday inside their homes on a rocky West Bank hillside by a group of violent Israeli settlers, who set up a tent in the front yard of one of the houses. Residents say about 10 to 15 settlers have been attacking them around the clock, throwing stones and an ax.

Early Wednesday morning, after news of the siege began to draw news attention, the Israeli army’s commander for the West Bank, Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, showed up in the village of Qusra and listened as one of the families described how the settlers had been terrorizing them since January. Outside, his soldiers tried to disperse the settlers with tear gas.

Yet, by 10:20 a.m., videos from security cameras show, the soldiers had left. Soon after, residents said, the settlers resumed their attacks.

“We had some hope in the morning when we saw that the army was present,” Aisha Hassan, 35, who was in the meeting with General Bluth, said by telephone, even as she said one of the settlers was throwing stones at her. “But when we saw that the army could not stop the settlers — now, honestly, we are more afraid.”

On Wednesday evening, the army said in response that it was assigning an extra battalion to the West Bank to try to “strengthen order and operational control in the area.”

The army’s initial retreat and broader struggle to contend with settler violence cast a spotlight on the increasingly chaotic situation in the West Bank, where hundreds of Israeli settlers have been terrorizing Palestinians with near-impunity all year.

As of late July, 18 Palestinians have been killed by settlers, one more than in all of 2025, according to U.N. data. Settlers have been boasting on social media of their attacks, posting videos showing mosques that have been torched in Palestinian towns.

At times, soldiers have taken part in the violence, Palestinian and Israeli officials say, reflecting disciplinary problems that the military has acknowledged are an issue.

“It’s a great fiasco,” said Gadi Shamni, a retired two-star general and former head of Israel’s Central Command, whose area of responsibility included the occupied territory. “There’s a loss of control over the West Bank.”

Israel’s right-wing, pro-settler government says that concerns about settler violence are overblown, and officials have repeatedly signaled their support for Israelis accused of attacks. The defense minister, Israel Katz, boasts of having stripped the army of the authority to issue detention orders for settlers — which had been a key tool for restraining Israeli extremist violence. In July, he visited in prison a settler arrested as a key suspect in the sexual assault of a Palestinian man in March and clashed with General Bluth over the suspect’s detention.

In Qusra, located near the city of Nablus in the northern West Bank, the violence has afflicted two families in particular: the Hassans and their neighbors the Abu Ridis.

Louai Abu Ridi, 46, a native of Qusra who immigrated to Ohio in 2003 and is a U.S. citizen in the gas-station business, said he had poured about $1 million into building a house in his birthplace. The settler attacks, beginning in January, started to lay waste to his investment, he said. His brother moved into the house to try to protect it.

Mr. Abu Ridi said he had appealed to the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem for help and was told to report the attacks to the Israeli authorities. An embassy spokesman did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

Ms. Hassan, whose brothers Yusuf and Rizq built two other homes on land owned by their father, said that settlers had broken windows and doors, cut utility lines, destroyed solar panels and stolen the birthday gifts a 2-year-old had received days earlier.

Residents said the settlers appeared to be based in an unfinished home outside Qusra. In March, witnesses said, settlers based in that same home killed another Qusra man, Amir Odeh, and beat and stabbed his father.

Sometimes the settlers have tried to intimidate the families, grazing sheep on their land and destroying their plantings. But the violence has escalated, Ms. Hassan said. Settlers once tried to push the family’s cooking-gas tank into the house through an open window, she said. They’ve fired gunshots and thrown Molotov cocktails at the house, she added.

Efforts by New York Times reporters on Wednesday to reach the scene and speak with the settlers and residents were rendered fruitless by roadblocks guarded by soldiers and settlers.

On Sunday, after the settlers set up camp just outside the Hassans’ homes and erected a tent, the family called the police. When an Israeli soldier showed up, Ms. Hassan said, he ignored the family and instead greeted the settlers warmly. Video recordings show him joining the settlers in prayers.

On Monday night, when Ms. Hassan’s 2-year-old niece, Hoor, spiked a fever and the family called an ambulance, she said, settlers blocked the ambulance and, the driver said, tried to ram it with an all-terrain vehicle. Late Tuesday afternoon, other soldiers made it possible for another ambulance to take the girl to a local clinic, Ms. Hassan recounted.

The military issued a statement on Tuesday acknowledging reports of Israelis seizing Palestinian homes and land in Qusra and expressing “condemnation” for what it called “illegal, reprehensible and unacceptable” actions. On Wednesday, it said that disciplinary action would be taken against the “security personnel involved.”

General Shamni, the retired Central Command chief, said that what had allowed him to keep the Israeli-occupied West Bank relatively calm during his tenure, from 2007 to 2009 — close cooperation with the Israeli police, the Internal Security Agency and the military’s Civil Administration — could no longer be counted on. Pro-settler extremists, like the cabinet ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, wield too much influence over all those agencies, General Shamni said.

Moreover, he added, the military units serving in the West Bank are largely composed of soldiers who grew up in the settlements. “They are the settlers,” he said. “That’s the problem.”

General Shamni said he wished that President Trump would force Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has minimized settler violence, to crack down on it.

General Bluth’s visit to Qusra on Wednesday appeared to signal a new resolve to address the situation, but it evidently alarmed the settlers. The young men who had been attacking the Qusra homes were quickly joined by scores more, who could be seen throwing stones onto the road to make it impassable and then scuffling with soldiers, according to witnesses and video viewed by a reporter.

Soldiers confiscated a tarp and an all-terrain vehicle but ultimately drove off, leaving the settlers behind.

They were still there on Wednesday night.

Gabby Sobelman contributed reporting.

item.title: Arabian Sea Bird and Turtle Habitat Threatened by Oil From Grounded Tanker
item.description:
An oil spill from a Russian shadow fleet tanker that ran aground two months ago has spread its long, black tongue across a remote, ecologically sensitive swath of the Arabian Sea, according to satellite data and statements from Oman’s government.

The spill has encircled the rocky cliffs of an Omani island, Jazirat al Qibliyah, that is home to a range of endangered seabirds, and spread to a 25-mile stretch of beach on the mainland, called Ras Madrakah, Oman’s environmental agency said Wednesday in a statement carried by the state news agency.

A British maritime disaster management company, called Ambrey, has been hired to rescue the tanker and stop the spread of the spill, according to the company. “This is an extremely challenging situation, compounded by adverse weather conditions,” said Ed Wollaston, director of global response at Ambrey.

The spill compounds the environmental consequences of three widening, overlapping conflicts that have made oil and gas infrastructure targets of war in recent months. Russia and Ukraine have attacked each other’s energy facilities. In Yemen, the Houthi militia has attacked oil tankers tied to Saudi Arabia. And the United States and Iran have attacked oil installations and tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

Several oil spills have been detected from satellite images in the strait, including a fairly significant one off Iran’s Kharg island, according to Brian Barnes, a geographer at the University of South Florida. None of them are anywhere near as large as the massive spills of the 1991 Gulf war, when Iraqi forces set ablaze hundreds of oil wells and caused one of the world’s worst environmental catastrophes, which took years to clean up. But swift cleanups are impossible with the ongoing conflict, and even the ecological impacts of the spills are hard to gauge at the moment.

“Satellite observations are great and can tell us a lot,” Mr. Barnes said. “But we don’t have the capacity to go out and see.”

On Tuesday, Iranian state media posted images of oil contamination spreading to Qeshm Island, including an area, known as Shib Deraz, where the rare hawksbill sea turtle nests every spring. Iranian government officials have said nothing about the cause of that spill.

The spill in Omani waters appears to be among the largest of several in the waterways of the Middle East. Estimates vary widely on the scale of the contamination, and what caused it in the first place remains a mystery. All that is certain is that Oman’s government has been forced to respond, because the tanker crashed into the rocky shoals of Qibliyah on a windy day in June.

It seems to have had little to do with Oman, or the conflicts in the region.

The tanker, known as the Caroline Bezengi, is about 900 feet long and capable of carrying nearly a million barrels of oil. It had been used for the last couple of years to ferry Russian crude oil to refineries in Asia, according to TankerTrackers.com, a company that monitors global oil shipping.

In the past, it was flagged under Cameroon. Its managing agent was a firm registered in Cyprus, called Lagosmarine, which was under sanctions by the United States and European Union for helping finance Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Since May, 2023, it had made 12 trips from ports in Russia to ports in India and Pakistan, and once to China, according to logs kept by TankerTrackers.com. In 2025, its crew had complained of not being paid for months, the Seafarers Union of Russia told Russian media outlets.

Its latest journey began on May 13 from the Russian port of Novorossiysk, on the Black Sea, according to TankerTrackers.com. It was headed for Sikka, a port on the western coast of India that serves the world’s largest refinery complex, near Jamnagar.

India, which has not signed on to Western sanctions imposed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, has instead sharply increased its purchase of Russian oil since that war began in 2022.

India’s growing economy needs a lot of oil, and its refineries, including the Jamnagar complex, have made a thriving business from exporting refined products to fuel-hungry countries.

The Caroline Bezengi did not reach India this time.

On June 6, the ship encountered “an incident” outside Oman’s territorial waters, the head of the country’s Environment Authority, Abdullah Bin Ali Al Amri, said in an interview on Oman TV.

Whether the incident was caused by malfunctioning equipment on the ship or by an attack remains unknown. No party has accepted responsibility.

By June 21, according to the Omani government, the ship ran aground on the rocks of the Qibliyah Island. “Reconnaissance measures were taken to inspect the ship’s safety, and indeed, at that time, there was no noticeable oil spill,” Mr. Al Amri said in the television interview.

By late July, there was a noticeable spill. By early August, it had spread.

Oman’s Environment Authority said this week that the slick covers around 390 square kilometers.

Greenpeace said that by Aug. 4 it had covered 600 square kilometers, a fourfold increase in just two days. “The situation surrounding the tanker Caroline Bezengi is yet another alarming example of the serious environmental risks posed by Russia’s so-called shadow fleet,” the organization said in a statement.

John Amos, head of an organization called SkyTruth, which uses satellite imagery to track oil contamination, estimated the coverage area to have grown to roughly 2,200 square kilometers. He said the Omani government’s estimate appears “far too low.”

Mr. Amos said if all of the Caroline Bezengi’s oil leaked, the spill would be comparable to the Exxon Valdez disaster, one of the worst spills in American history that killed hundreds of thousands of seabirds, otters, seals and whales.

Ambrey, the maritime response firm, said in a statement to The New York Times that it was working with the Omani Air Force to stabilize the ship and that ships to help with the salvage operation were en route.

Shadow fleet tankers are often uninsured, and shipowners rarely come forward. Oman is left with the task of monitoring and stanching the damage. The Environment Authority, in its latest statement on Monday, said the slick was advancing quickly in a northeasterly direction.

It said it was trying to protect the most environmentally sensitive areas. “Efforts are being directed towards identifying zones most vulnerable to impact and correlating them with pollution drift trajectories, with particular emphasis on areas of high ecological value and sensitivity,” the ministry said.

Zane Irwin and Ismaeel Naar contributed reporting

item.title: How Raúl Castro’s Grandson Rose From Bodyguard to Key Power Broker
item.description:
Raúl Castro was on an official state visit in Paris a decade ago as Cuba’s president when a hulky bodyguard in his entourage stood out.

The man kept so close to Mr. Castro while they walked the red carpet at the Élysée Palace that a member of the French honor guard tried pulling him back.

Even François Hollande, France’s president at the time, waved him back.

The security escort who kept inserting himself in official photos was none other than Mr. Castro’s grandson, Raúl G. Rodríguez Castro, a colonel in the interior ministry.

Today, the once largely unknown bodyguard has become a key figure in Cuba’s talks with the United States, even though he has never held public office. His name has even come up as someone the Trump administration might find acceptable to become Cuba’s next leader.

“He exemplifies how that government operates,” said Tim Rieser, a foreign policy aide to former Senator Patrick Leahy, a Democrat from Vermont, who met Mr. Rodríguez Castro several times. “It’s a lot like a family business, and so someone who was described to us a decade ago as President Castro’s bodyguard has for whatever reason, by whatever means, become something much more than that.”

But Mr. Rodríguez Castro, who has met with some of the most senior people in the Trump administration, may have also used his considerable influence to protect a large-scale smuggling operation that moved people out of Cuba and brought illicit goods into the country, according to interviews and court records.

Mr. Rodríguez Castro, 42, was accused of helping funnel goods purchased with stolen credit cards into the country, receiving luxury items as bribes and allowing wanted criminals to roam free on the island, the interviews and court records show.

The scheme was the target of a federal investigation that resulted in the convictions of at least 21 people and decades-long sentences. Mr. Rodríguez Castro has not been charged.

This article is based on court documents and interviews with nearly a dozen people who either know Mr. Rodríguez Castro personally, including one person close to the U.S. negotiations, or are familiar with the criminal investigation in which his name surfaced.

Mr. Rodríguez Castro did not respond to requests for an interview sent through formal diplomatic channels and a mutual acquaintance. A top Cuban official called the accusations slanderous.

Mr. Rodríguez Castro’s prominent role in the discussions with the Trump administration seemed to astound some Cuban officials who viewed him as merely a caretaker for his grandfather.

Still, an official with the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Cuba took to social media last month to say Mr. Rodríguez Castro had been the subject of “character assassination” in the U.S. media, which was aimed at making the Cuban government appear divided.

As he helps Cuba’s government try to survive and navigate its standoff with the United States, those who have spoken to Mr. Rodríguez Castro say he has made no secret of his ultimate ambition to be his country’s next president — though it is unclear whether he has the internal support to do so.

The human smuggling network was known as the Cuban Mafia in Quintana Roo; its name came from the state in eastern Mexico where it was based.

The ring used boats stolen from Florida to sneak people out of Cuba who wanted to reach the United States, according to the Justice Department and members of the criminal gang who cooperated with prosecutors.

The Cuban migrants would be taken to Mexico, where they were held in safe houses until they paid smuggling fees, and were tortured if they didn’t, according to court testimony.

Two defendants in the case implicated Mr. Rodríguez Castro as a collaborator in the organization, according to court records and interviews with several people familiar with the investigation. Both defendants, José Miguel González Vidal and Reynaldo Crespo Márquez, pleaded guilty and were sentenced to long prison terms for their roles in the scheme.

Mr. Rodríguez Castro arranged safe passage for the group into and out of Cuba, a leader of the group told U.S. prosecutors, several people familiar with the case said. Mr. Rodríguez Castro’s name came up in a U.S. Department of Justice case in 2020 against the group, according to evidence gathered by prosecutors and one of the people familiar with the investigation.

The people who know Mr. Rodríguez Castro spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve relationships with Cuban government officials, and those familiar with the criminal case did so to discuss sensitive legal matters they were not authorized to disclose.

It is unclear whether Mr. Rodríguez Castro is a target of the ongoing investigation. The Justice Department declined to comment.

The smuggling ring stole vessels from South Florida to bribe foreign officials, according to an admission statement filed in federal court as part of a guilty plea signed by Mr. González Vidal, who was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

The statement does not name Mr. Rodríguez Castro.

But Mr. González Vidal and another defendant told U.S. authorities that Mr. Rodríguez Castro was among the foreign officials who received a stolen boat, court records show.

The issue was also discussed in open court.

During a September 2023 trial in Miami, a defense lawyer asked Mr. Crespo, who was a cooperating witness, about a meeting in which he told prosecutors that Mr. González Vidal and Mr. Rodríguez Castro had discussed sending him a boat in Cuba. Mr. Crespo is serving 20 years in prison for his role in the smuggling operation.

Mr. González-Vidal said the men who smuggled migrants and goods bribed Mr. Rodríguez Castro to keep the Cuban Coast Guard and Customs away, three of the people said.

In exchange for allowing merchandise that the smuggling network bought in Mexico with stolen credit cards to clear Cuban customs, Mr. Rodríguez Castro was given a Fountain 38 high-performance boat and various other gifts, including a Rolex watch, Suzuki motorbike and Louis Vuitton clothes, Mr. González Vidal claimed.

The products were later sold in Cuban government stores, he said.

Mr. González Vidal’s account was supported by text and voice mail messages that the F.B.I. extracted from the cellphones of members of the smuggling ring, the people familiar with the case said.

Mr. González Vidal’s lawyer, Juan D. Berrios, declined to comment.

Mr. Rodríguez Castro, in a recent interview with USA Today, which some critics took to be self-promotional, he said he had no wealth of his own. “Wealthy friends and admirers” had paid for fashionable clothes, luxury foreign vehicles and expensive overseas trips, he said.

Cuba’s deputy foreign minister, Carlos R. Fernández de Cossío, in an interview with The Times in Havana, called the accusations against Mr. Rodríguez Castro involving the smuggling ring “slander.”

He said that for several years during migration talks with the United States, Cuban officials had repeatedly raised concerns about widespread smuggling of Cubans through Central America and Mexico.

They received no response, he said.

“We alerted them. Meeting after meeting: ‘Have you taken action? What have you done?’” Mr. Fernández de Cossío said. “I cannot doubt whatsoever that there are organizations in Mexico, in Central America and in other parts of Latin America, which involve Cubans that have been making money and had a business of smuggling aliens to the United States.

“But I can assure you,” he added, “there’s no link with the Cuban government.”

The State Department did not respond to a request for comment.

One American close to the U.S.-Cuba discussions said that, despite the allegations of smuggling, Mr. Rodríguez Castro was considered a worthy representative to interact with the Trump administration because his fondness for material goods suggested he was open to capitalist ideas.

Mr. Rodríguez Castro is not apologetic about his lifestyle.

“It pains me that many people can’t live the way I do,” Mr. Rodríguez Castro told USA Today. “And I’m working every day to change that situation.”

Mr. Rodríguez Castro is the son of Raúl Castro’s eldest daughter, Déborah Castro Espín, and the late Gen. Luis Alberto Rodríguez López-Calleja, a powerful figure who helped establish Cuba’s military conglomerate, known as GAESA, which manages much of Cuba’s ailing economy.

His parents had a troubled marriage, so Mr. Rodríguez Castro, who is also known as “Raulito,” spent much of his youth at his grandparents’ house, several people who knew him in his youth said. His nickname, which is how he is commonly known, is “el Cangrejo,” meaning “the crab,” and was given to him because he was born with an extra finger on one hand.

Despite his revolutionary roots, he is descended from an upper-class family — his grandmother was an heir to the Bacardi rum fortune. He enjoyed extreme sports, music with racy lyrics and was less polished than other members of Cuba’s revolutionary elite.

He studied economics at the University of Havana, where he received credit for traveling with his grandfather, said Juan Juan Almeida, the exiled son of a hero of the 1959 Cuban revolution who was close to the Castro family for many years.

He described Mr. Rodríguez Castro as affectionate and friendly.

“He is better known outside Cuba than inside,” he said. “Cangrejo and all the Castros know that their power only lasts until the day his grandfather dies.”

Mr. Rodríguez Castro, who is often photographed wearing expensive designer clothes, was widely known during his younger years for being spotted in videos partying at concerts, hanging out with the reggaeton duo Gente de Zona and on boats.

One family member said he sometimes traveled around Havana in one of his grandfather’s BMWs, which irked some who thought it projected a bad image in a country where people suffer severe food, medicine and power shortages.

Mr. Rodríguez Castro has enjoyed extraordinary access, attending virtually every one of his grandfather’s meetings, including with the late Pope Francis.

After serving as a bodyguard, he became more of a personal assistant for Mr. Castro, 95, who was vice president for decades and became president in 2006 when his brother Fidel fell ill. While he no longer holds any official government post, Mr. Castro is widely considered the most powerful person in Cuba.

After Cuba began secret meetings with the United States this year seeking to end sanctions imposed by the Trump administration, Mr. Rodríguez Castro met separately with C.I.A. Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. (The C.I.A. has covertly created a task force as part of the U.S. campaign to pressure Cuba into political, economic and leadership change, The Times reported.)

Arturo Lopez-Levy, a research associate at the University of Denver who is a second cousin to Mr. Rodríguez Castro, said much of the criticism of his relative is based on videos of rowdy behavior that circulated more than a decade ago.

He has not spoken to his cousin in about seven or eight years, he said, but his public persona appears to have changed considerably.

“The relationship with his grandfather has changed from a young man who was quite immature to someone with political knowledge and connection to his grandfather — not only for the protection of his life, but politically,” said Mr. Lopez-Levy, a former analyst at Cuba’s Ministry of Interior. “He has not been outside the door; he has been inside every meeting.”

Reporting was contributed by David Ovalle and Jack Nicas. Seamus Hughes and Kristen Noyes contributed research.
